claim: The collection includes high-quality whole genome assemblies of 1180 isolates of CC398.
source: Our collection includes high-quality whole genome assemblies of 1180 isolates (including 43 complete reference genomes).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the dataset.

claim: The CC398 collection spans 15 host species including humans, pigs, cows, chickens, turkeys, and horses.
source: This collection spans 15 host species (including humans, pigs, cows, chickens, turkeys, and horses), 28 countries (across Europe, America, Asia, and Australasia), and 27 years (1992–2018) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the dataset.

claim: The CC398 collection spans 28 countries across Europe, America, Asia, and Australasia.
source: This collection spans 15 host species (including humans, pigs, cows, chickens, turkeys, and horses), 28 countries (across Europe, America, Asia, and Australasia), and 27 years (1992–2018) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the dataset.

claim: The CC398 collection spans 27 years from 1992 to 2018.
source: This collection spans 15 host species (including humans, pigs, cows, chickens, turkeys, and horses), 28 countries (across Europe, America, Asia, and Australasia), and 27 years (1992–2018) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the dataset.

claim: The phylogenetic reconstruction shows a livestock-associated clade of CC398 containing 704 isolates that falls within a more diverse, largely human-associated clade containing 476 isolates.
source: These reconstructions consistently returned the same topology, and one that is described in previous studies: a livestock-associated clade of CC398 (704 isolates) that falls within a more diverse, and other largely human-associated clade (476 isolates) (Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Price et al., 2012; Gonçalves da Silva et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1a, with citation to previous studies.

claim: Livestock-associated CC398 originated around 1964 with a 95% confidence interval of 1957-1970.
source: This led to an estimate of the origin of the livestock-associated clade of approximately 1964 (95% CI: 1957–1970) (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Stated in text based on dated phylogeny analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The evolutionary rate of CC398 is estimated at 1.1–1.6 × 10−6 substitutions per site per year.
source: Our estimates of the evolutionary rate were consistent across all reconstructions (1.1–1.6 × 10−6 subs/site/year), and similar to estimates from previous studies of CC398 (Ward et al., 2014) and other S. aureus CCs (Hsu et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated in text based on BEAST analysis, with citation to previous studies showing similar rates.

claim: The transition to livestock association is associated with changes in the frequencies of three MGEs: a Tn916 transposon carrying tetM, SCCmec carrying mecA, and φSa3 prophages carrying a human immune evasion gene cluster.
source: We find that the genes whose presence most strongly distinguishes isolates from the human- and livestock-associated groups are associated with three categories of MGEs: (1) a Tn916 transposon carrying tetM, (2) SCCmec carrying mecA, and (3) φSa3 prophages carrying a human immune evasion gene cluster (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 5, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Stated in text based on comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 1a.

claim: A Tn916 transposon carrying tetM is present in 699 out of 704 isolates in the livestock-associated CC398 collection.
source: We identified a contiguous assembly of a Tn916 transposon carrying tetM in 699/704 isolates in our collection of livestock-associated CC398 (Figure 2a, Supplementary files 3 and 4; de Vries et al., 2009; Roberts and Mullany, 2009).
evidence: Stated in text based on assembly analysis, with citations to previous studies characterizing this element.

claim: The Tn916 transposon in livestock-associated CC398 is the result of a single acquisition event followed by stable inheritance.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate that the presence of the Tn916 transposon in livestock-associated CC398 is the result of a single acquisition event, followed by stable inheritance.
evidence: Stated in text based on multiple lines of evidence including conserved location, nucleotide diversity, and phylogenetic congruence.

claim: The location of the Tn916 transposon in the genome of livestock-associated CC398 is conserved, always found next to the same core gene (WP_000902814 in the published annotation of S0385).
source: First, the location of the transposon in the genome of livestock-associated CC398 is conserved (Tn916 is always found next to the same core gene; WP_000902814 in the published annotation of S0385).
evidence: Stated in text based on analysis of de novo assemblies.

claim: The Tn916 transposon shows similar average nucleotide diversity to core genes in livestock-associated CC398.
source: Second, an alignment of the coding regions of this element (extracted from de novo assemblies) shows a similar average nucleotide diversity to core genes (Figure 2d).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 2d comparing nucleotide diversity.

claim: A phylogeny constructed from the genes in the Tn916 transposon is entirely congruent with the phylogeny of livestock-associated CC398.
source: Third, a phylogeny constructed from the genes in this element is entirely congruent with the phylogeny of livestock-associated CC398 (Figure 2b, c).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 2b and 2c comparing phylogenies.

claim: The Tn916 transposon has been maintained in livestock-associated CC398 for around 57 years.
source: Our analyses indicate that the Tn916 transposon has been maintained in livestock-associated CC398 since its origin, and therefore for around 57 years (Figure 1b).
evidence: Stated in text based on dated phylogeny shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The Tn916 transposon is absent from 5 out of 704 livestock-associated CC398 isolates, suggesting it remains capable of excision.
source: Nevertheless, its absence from 5/704 livestock-associated CC398 isolates in our collection suggests that it remains capable of excision (this is consistent with experimental studies that have shown that Tn916 in CC398 is a functional conjugative transposon; de Vries et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated in text based on data analysis, with citation to experimental studies.

claim: SCCmec elements in CC398 are categorized into type V (76%) and type IV (21%).
source: Consistent with previous studies of CC398 (e.g. Price et al., 2012), we observe both type V (76%) and type IV (21%) in CC398 (we were unable to confidently type the remaining 3%; Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary files 3 and 5).
evidence: Stated in text based on SCCmec typing analysis, with citation to previous studies.

claim: Most type V SCCmec elements belong to the subtype Vc previously described in livestock-associated CC398.
source: Most of the type V SCCmec elements belong to the subtype Vc previously described in livestock-associated CC398 (Li et al., 2011; Price et al., 2012; Vandendriessche et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to previous studies describing this subtype.

claim: The type Vc SCCmec element includes three resistance genes: tetK (tetracycline resistance), czrC (heavy metal resistance), and mecA (methicillin resistance).
source: This element includes two additional resistance genes: tetK (tetracycline resistance) and czrC (heavy metal resistance) (Figure 3a and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 3a gene map. mecA is mentioned earlier as being carried by SCCmec.

claim: A full-length version of the type Vc SCCmec element was identified in 335 genomes.
source: We identified a full-length version of this element in 335 genomes (including some of the most recent isolates in our collection, sampled from UK pig farms in 2018) and shorter type V elements in 204 genomes.
evidence: Stated in text based on assembly analysis.

claim: Shorter type V SCCmec elements were found in 204 genomes.
source: We identified a full-length version of this element in 335 genomes (including some of the most recent isolates in our collection, sampled from UK pig farms in 2018) and shorter type V elements in 204 genomes.
evidence: Stated in text based on assembly analysis.

claim: Full-length type Vc SCCmec elements are only observed in the livestock-associated clade.
source: Full-length versions are only observed in the livestock-associated clade, while shorter versions are found in both livestock- and human-associated groups of CC398.
evidence: Stated in text based on analysis of element distribution across clades.

claim: Shorter type V SCCmec elements are found in both livestock- and human-associated groups of CC398.
source: Full-length versions are only observed in the livestock-associated clade, while shorter versions are found in both livestock- and human-associated groups of CC398.
evidence: Stated in text based on analysis of element distribution across clades.

claim: Shorter type V SCCmec elements often lacked tetK (n = 90) and czrC (n = 117) genes.
source: Shorter versions often lacked tetK (n = 90) and czrC (n = 117) genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in text based on gene content analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Type IV SCCmec elements are only observed in the livestock-associated clade.
source: Type IV elements are only observed in the livestock-associated clade.
evidence: Stated in text based on analysis of element distribution.

claim: Type IV SCCmec elements include subtypes IVa and IVc and all only carry a single resistance gene: mecA.
source: They include subtypes IVa and IVc, and all only carry a single resistance gene: mecA.
evidence: Stated in text based on analysis of gene content in type IV elements.

claim: Type Vc SCCmec is more common in pigs (77% of isolates) than type IV SCCmec (7% of isolates).
source: Type Vc SCCmec is much more common in pigs (77% of isolates; n = 286) than type IV SCCmec (7% of isolates).
evidence: Stated in text based on analysis of element frequencies across host species.

claim: In cows, 45% of isolates carry type Vc SCCmec and 32% carry type IV SCCmec.
source: In cows (n = 74), the difference is reduced: 45% are type Vc and 32% are type IV.
evidence: Stated in text based on analysis of element frequencies in cow isolates.

claim: In isolates from other animal species, type IV SCCmec elements (55%) are more common than type Vc (33%).
source: And in isolates from other animal species (n = 94) type IV elements (55%) are more common than type Vc (33%).
evidence: Stated in text based on analysis of element frequencies in other animal species.

claim: A full-length type Vc SCCmec was acquired once by livestock-associated CC398 and has been maintained largely through vertical transmission.
source: Diversity within the type Vc SCCmec element indicates that a full-length type Vc SCCmec was acquired once by livestock-associated CC398, and has been maintained within CC398 largely through vertical transmission.
evidence: Stated in text based on multiple lines of evidence including nucleotide diversity and phylogenetic congruence.

claim: Low nucleotide diversity within full-length versions of the type Vc SCCmec element is consistent with 329 out of 335 sharing a recent origin common within livestock-associated CC398.
source: First, low nucleotide diversity within full-length versions of the element is consistent with 329/335 sharing a recent origin common within livestock-associated CC398 (Figure 3d).
evidence: Stated in text based on nucleotide diversity analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Patterns of diversity in the type Vc SCCmec element are largely congruent with the core genome phylogeny, consistent with vertical inheritance.
source: Second, patterns of diversity are largely congruent with the core genome phylogeny, consistent with vertical inheritance (Figure 3b, c).
evidence: Stated in text based on phylogenetic comparison shown in Figure 3b and 3c.

claim: Low nucleotide diversity within genes shared across full- and shorter-length versions of the type V SCCmec element is consistent with most shorter-length versions being the result of deletion within livestock-associated CC398.
source: Third, low nucleotide diversity within genes shared across full- and shorter-length versions of the element are consistent with most shorter-length versions being the result of deletion within livestock-associated CC398 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in text based on nucleotide diversity analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Diversity in the type IV SCCmec elements in livestock-associated CC398 supports four independent acquisitions from outside of CC398.
source: In contrast, diversity in the type IV elements in livestock-associated CC398 supports four independent acquisitions from outside of CC398 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Stated in text based on diversity analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The type Vc SCCmec was acquired by livestock-associated CC398 by around 1986 (95% CI: 1982–1990).
source: These reconstructions consistently estimated that the type Vc SCCmec had been acquired by livestock-associated CC398 by around 1986 (95% CI: 1982–1990), and has therefore been maintained within livestock-associated CC398 for around 35 years.
evidence: Stated in text based on ancestral state reconstruction over dated phylogeny.

claim: The type Vc SCCmec has been maintained within livestock-associated CC398 for around 35 years.
source: These reconstructions consistently estimated that the type Vc SCCmec had been acquired by livestock-associated CC398 by around 1986 (95% CI: 1982–1990), and has therefore been maintained within livestock-associated CC398 for around 35 years.
evidence: Stated in text based on ancestral state reconstruction and dating analysis.

claim: Type IV SCCmec elements show evidence of several acquisitions in relatively quick succession between 1997 and 2004.
source: In contrast, type IV elements show evidence of several more recent acquisitions in relatively quick succession between 1997 and 2004 (Figure 3e and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Stated in text based on ancestral state reconstruction shown in Figure 3e and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: φSa3 prophages are present in 88% of the human-associated CC398 isolates.
source: While φSa3 prophages are present in 88% of the human-associated CC398 isolates in our collection, we find that this is not a consequence of a stable association between CC398 and one prophage.
evidence: Stated in text based on analysis of prophage presence.

claim: Nucleotide diversity within genes shared across φSa3 prophages suggests at least seven (but likely more) acquisitions of an φSa3 prophage into human-associated CC398 from outside of CC398.
source: Nucleotide diversity within genes shared across φSa3 prophages (Figure 4 and Supplementary file 3) suggest at least seven (but likely more) acquisitions of an φSa3 prophage into human-associated CC398 from outside of CC398.
evidence: Stated in text based on nucleotide diversity analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: φSa3 prophages within human-associated CC398 include types C (n = 285), B (n = 111), E (n = 35), A (n = 4), and D (n = 4).
source: The set of functional genes carried by these elements indicate that the elements within human-associated CC398 include types C (n = 285), B (n = 111), E (n = 35), A (n = 4), and D (n = 4), and those carried by livestock-associated CC398 isolates include types B (n = 84), E (n = 8), and A (n = 5) (van Wamel et al., 2006; van Alen et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in text based on functional gene analysis, with citations to previous typing studies.

claim: φSa3 prophages carried by livestock-associated CC398 isolates include types B (n = 84), E (n = 8), and A (n = 5).
source: The set of functional genes carried by these elements indicate that the elements within human-associated CC398 include types C (n = 285), B (n = 111), E (n = 35), A (n = 4), and D (n = 4), and those carried by livestock-associated CC398 isolates include types B (n = 84), E (n = 8), and A (n = 5) (van Wamel et al., 2006; van Alen et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in text based on functional gene analysis, with citations to previous typing studies.

claim: φSa3 prophages are rare in livestock-associated CC398, present in 68 out of 704 isolates.
source: While φSa3 prophages are rare in livestock-associated CC398 (68/704 isolates), diversity within these elements indicate at least 15 (but likely more) acquisitions of these MGEs by livestock-associated CC398.
evidence: Stated in text based on analysis of prophage presence.

claim: Diversity within φSa3 prophages in livestock-associated CC398 indicates at least 15 (but likely more) acquisitions of these MGEs by livestock-associated CC398.
source: While φSa3 prophages are rare in livestock-associated CC398 (68/704 isolates), diversity within these elements indicate at least 15 (but likely more) acquisitions of these MGEs by livestock-associated CC398.
evidence: Stated in text based on diversity analysis.

claim: The majority (69%) of φSa3 prophages in livestock-associated CC398 do not share a recent common ancestor with those in human-associated CC398.
source: The majority of these elements (69%) do not share a recent common ancestor with those in human-associated CC398.
evidence: Stated in text based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: A poultry-associated subclade of livestock-associated CC398 contains 51 isolates, with 39% from poultry compared to 4% across the rest of the livestock-associated clade.
source: In our collection, 39% of the isolates in this clade are from poultry (compared to 4% across the rest of the livestock-associated clade).
evidence: Stated in text based on analysis of host species distribution.

claim: Low nucleotide diversity within the type B φSa3 consistently present in the poultry-associated subclade suggests it has been maintained since its acquisition approximately 21 years ago (95% CI: 1997–2001).
source: Low nucleotide diversity within the type B φSa3 consistently present in isolates within this clade suggests that it has been maintained since its acquisition approximately 21 years ago (95% CI: 1997–2001; Figure 1b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in text based on nucleotide diversity analysis and dating, shown in Figure 1b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 81% of livestock-associated CC398 isolates carry one or more resistance genes for antibiotic classes other than tetracyclines and β-lactams.
source: We see evidence of this in our dataset where 81% of livestock-associated CC398 isolates carry one or more resistance genes for antibiotic classes other than tetracyclines and β-lactams (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Stated in text based on resistance gene analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: 67% of livestock-associated CC398 isolates have genes associated with trimethoprim resistance (dfrA, dfrK, or dfrG).
source: Sixty-seven percent of livestock-associated CC398 isolates have genes associated with trimethoprim resistance (dfrA, dfrK, or dfrG), 42% have genes associated with macrolide resistance (ermA, ermB, ermC, or ermT), and 26% have genes associated with aminoglycoside resistance (aadA, aphA, or aphD).
evidence: Stated in text based on resistance gene analysis.

claim: 42% of livestock-associated CC398 isolates have genes associated with macrolide resistance (ermA, ermB, ermC, or ermT).
source: Sixty-seven percent of livestock-associated CC398 isolates have genes associated with trimethoprim resistance (dfrA, dfrK, or dfrG), 42% have genes associated with macrolide resistance (ermA, ermB, ermC, or ermT), and 26% have genes associated with aminoglycoside resistance (aadA, aphA, or aphD).
evidence: Stated in text based on resistance gene analysis.

claim: 26% of livestock-associated CC398 isolates have genes associated with aminoglycoside resistance (aadA, aphA, or aphD).
source: Sixty-seven percent of livestock-associated CC398 isolates have genes associated with trimethoprim resistance (dfrA, dfrK, or dfrG), 42% have genes associated with macrolide resistance (ermA, ermB, ermC, or ermT), and 26% have genes associated with aminoglycoside resistance (aadA, aphA, or aphD).
evidence: Stated in text based on resistance gene analysis.

claim: Only 20% of human-associated CC398 isolates carry tetracycline resistance genes.
source: Not only are resistance genes less common in human-associated CC398 (only 20% of isolates carry tetracycline resistance genes, and 9% carry trimethoprim resistance genes), they also differ in their relative frequencies.
evidence: Stated in text based on resistance gene analysis.

claim: 9% of human-associated CC398 isolates carry trimethoprim resistance genes.
source: Not only are resistance genes less common in human-associated CC398 (only 20% of isolates carry tetracycline resistance genes, and 9% carry trimethoprim resistance genes), they also differ in their relative frequencies.
evidence: Stated in text based on resistance gene analysis.

claim: Human-associated CC398 isolates more commonly carry genes associated with macrolide resistance (91%).
source: In particular, human-associated CC398 isolates more commonly carry genes associated with macrolide resistance (91%).
evidence: Stated in text based on resistance gene analysis.

claim: φSa3 prophages are more common in human isolates (23%) than in livestock or companion animal isolates (11%) in the livestock-associated CC398 collection.
source: φSa3 prophages are more common in human isolates (23%) than in livestock or companion animal isolates (11%) in our collection of livestock-associated CC398.
evidence: Stated in text based on analysis of prophage frequencies across host types.

claim: Isolates from humans are significantly more likely to carry an φSa3 prophage than isolates from livestock or companion animals (McNemar's chi-squared test: p = 1.50 × 10−3).
source: Comparisons across these groups revealed that isolates from humans are consistently more likely to carry an φSa3 prophage (McNemar's chi-squared test: p = 1.50 × 10−3; Figure 5).
evidence: Stated in text based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: No resistance gene was significantly more or less common in humans than in livestock species (McNemar's chi-squared tests: p > 0.1).
source: We find that no resistance gene was significantly more or less common in humans than in livestock species (McNemar's chi-squared tests: p > 0.1), nor was there a consistent shift in the overall number of resistance genes (there were more resistance genes in isolates from human hosts in 22/70 pairs and more in livestock hosts in 34/70 pairs).
evidence: Stated in text based on statistical analysis of resistance gene frequencies.

claim: There was no consistent shift in the overall number of resistance genes between human and livestock hosts (more resistance genes in isolates from human hosts in 22/70 pairs and more in livestock hosts in 34/70 pairs).
source: We find that no resistance gene was significantly more or less common in humans than in livestock species (McNemar's chi-squared tests: p > 0.1), nor was there a consistent shift in the overall number of resistance genes (there were more resistance genes in isolates from human hosts in 22/70 pairs and more in livestock hosts in 34/70 pairs).
evidence: Stated in text based on analysis of resistance gene counts.

claim: φSa3 prophages are less common in isolates from pigs (only 3% of pig isolates carry one) than from other non-human species.
source: φSa3 prophages are also less common in isolates from pigs than from other non-human species (only 3% of pig isolates carry one).
evidence: Stated in text based on analysis of prophage frequencies across host species.

claim: In 42 out of 70 phylogenetically independent groups where the only non-human species was a pig, none of the pig isolates carried an φSa3 prophage while 14% of the human isolates did.
source: In 42/70 of our phylogenetically independent groups, the only non-human species was a pig, and none of the pig isolates from these groups carried an φSa3 prophage (while 14% of the human isolates did).
evidence: Stated in text based on analysis of phylogenetically independent groups.

claim: In groups that included isolates from cows, horses, and poultry, φSa3 prophages were observed in non-human hosts in 17% of groups and at a higher frequency in humans (39% of groups) (McNemar's chi-squared test: p = 0.04).
source: In the remaining 28 groups (that included isolates from cows, horses, and poultry), φSa3 prophages were observed in non-human hosts in 17% of groups, but still at a higher frequency in humans (39% of groups) (McNemar's chi-squared test: p = 0.04).
evidence: Stated in text based on statistical analysis of prophage frequencies.

claim: MGEs play an important role in the evolution of bacterial pathogens.
source: Mobile genetic elements (MGEs) play an important role in the evolution of bacterial pathogens.
evidence: Stated in text as an introductory statement drawing on established scientific knowledge.

claim: MGEs often carry genes associated with virulence and antibiotic resistance.
source: As MGEs often carry genes associated with virulence and antibiotic resistance (Frost et al., 2005; Rankin et al., 2011), an understanding of the drivers and barriers to their acquisition and maintenance is central to predicting the emergence and evolution of novel and resistant pathogens (Brockhurst et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to previous studies.

claim: The emergence and evolution of MRSA across different ecological niches and host species are associated with the horizontal transfer of MGEs.
source: The emergence and evolution of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) across different ecological niches and host species are associated with the horizontal transfer of MGEs.
evidence: Stated in text as a general statement about MRSA evolution.

claim: Methicillin resistance is carried by the staphylococcal cassette chromosome element SCCmec.
source: Methicillin resistance is carried by the staphylococcal cassette chromosome element SCCmec, and additional MGEs carry resistance to other antibiotics, virulence factors, and host-specific adaptations (Hanssen and Ericson Sollid, 2006; Jamrozy et al., 2017; Haag et al., 2019; Turner et al., 2019; Matuszewska et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to previous studies.

claim: CC398 has become the dominant MRSA in European livestock.
source: CC398 has become the dominant MRSA in European livestock.
evidence: Stated in text as a factual statement about CC398 prevalence.

claim: The proportion of MRSA-positive herds in Danish pig farms increased from <5% in 2008 to 90% in 2018.
source: Its rise has been particularly evident in Danish pig farms where the proportion of MRSA-positive herds has increased from <5% in 2008 to 90% in 2018 (Sieber et al., 2018; DANMAP, 2019), but it has also been observed in other European countries, and other livestock species (Lekkerkerk et al., 2015; Islam et al., 2017; Anjum et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to surveillance reports.

claim: Livestock-associated MRSA CC398 has been associated with increasing numbers of human infections, in both people with and without direct contact with livestock.
source: Livestock-associated (LA) MRSA CC398 has been associated with increasing numbers of human infections, in both people with and without direct contact with livestock (Larsen et al., 2017; van Alen et al., 2017; Sieber et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies identified a largely methicillin-resistant and livestock-associated clade of CC398 that falls as either sister to or within a largely methicillin-sensitive and human-associated clade.
source: They identified a largely methicillin-resistant and livestock-associated clade of CC398, that falls as either sister to Ward et al., 2014 or within (Price et al., 2012; Gonçalves da Silva et al., 2017) a largely methicillin-sensitive and human-associated clade.
evidence: Stated in text with citations to previous phylogenetic studies.

claim: Previous studies concluded that the emergence of CC398 in livestock was associated with both the acquisition of antibiotic resistance genes and the loss of genes associated with human immune evasion.
source: Through comparing the genomes of isolates from livestock- and human-associated CC398, these studies concluded that the emergence of CC398 in livestock was associated with both the acquisition of antibiotic resistance genes and the loss of genes associated with human immune evasion.
evidence: Stated in text summarizing conclusions from previous studies.

claim: Antibiotics, including tetracyclines, were first licensed for use as growth promoters in livestock in European countries in the 1950s and were in common use by the end of that decade.
source: Antibiotics, including tetracyclines, were first licensed for use as growth promoters in livestock in European countries in the 1950s, and were in common use by the end of that decade (Lowbury, 1958).
evidence: Stated in text with citation to historical reference.

claim: The use of antibiotics as growth promoters was banned by the European Union in 2006.
source: While the use of antibiotics as growth promoters was banned by the European Union in 2006, tetracyclines remain the most commonly used antimicrobial class in livestock farming (World Health Organization, 2015; DANMAP, 2019).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to WHO and surveillance reports.

claim: Tetracyclines remain the most commonly used antimicrobial class in livestock farming.
source: While the use of antibiotics as growth promoters was banned by the European Union in 2006, tetracyclines remain the most commonly used antimicrobial class in livestock farming (World Health Organization, 2015; DANMAP, 2019).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to WHO and surveillance reports.

claim: Tn916-like elements are found across several bacterial genera including other opportunistic pathogens in the respiratory microbiome of pigs and other S. aureus CCs.
source: Tn916-like elements are found across several bacterial genera (Clewell et al., 1995; Roberts and Mullany, 2009), including other opportunistic pathogens in the respiratory microbiome of pigs (Holden et al., 2009; Hoa et al., 2011) and other S. aureus CCs (de Vries et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to previous studies.

claim: The regulatory system of Tn916 promotes its maintenance in a host through ensuring that excision only occurs in the presence of tetracycline (or other transcription-limiting cell stress) and that any selective burden in the absence of treatment is minimised.
source: Previous studies have found evidence that the regulatory system of Tn916 promotes its maintenance in a host through ensuring both that excision only occurs in the presence of tetracycline (or other transcription-limiting cell stress) and that any selective burden in the absence of treatment is minimised (Roberts and Mullany, 2009).
evidence: Stated in text with citation to previous study.

claim: Carrying tetK in addition to tetM is associated with increased fitness during exposure to sublethal concentrations of tetracycline.
source: While all livestock-associated CC398 carry tetM, there is evidence that carrying tetK in addition to tetM is associated with increased fitness during exposure to sublethal concentrations of tetracycline (Larsen et al., 2016a).
evidence: Stated in text with citation to previous study.

claim: czrC is associated with heavy metal resistance.
source: czrC is associated with heavy metal resistance (Cavaco et al., 2010), which is likely to be beneficial in the context of the common supplementation of animal feed with zinc oxide, which in pigs is commonly used to prevent diarrhoea in weaners (Nielsen et al., 2021).
evidence: Stated in text with citation to previous study.

claim: Zinc oxide is commonly used in pig feed to prevent diarrhoea in weaners.
source: czrC is associated with heavy metal resistance (Cavaco et al., 2010), which is likely to be beneficial in the context of the common supplementation of animal feed with zinc oxide, which in pigs is commonly used to prevent diarrhoea in weaners (Nielsen et al., 2021).
evidence: Stated in text with citation to previous study.

claim: The SCCmec type Vc element has been found in other staphylococci (S. cohhii in Vervet Monkeys) but has not been reported in other S. aureus CCs.
source: The element has been found in other staphylococci (S. cohhii in Vervet Monkeys [Hoefer et al., 2021]), but has not been reported in other S. aureus CCs.
evidence: Stated in text with citation to previous study.

claim: φSa3 prophages carry human immune evasion gene clusters that include a variable set of functional genes that encode human-specific virulence factors, including sak, chp, scn, sea, and sep.
source: φSa3 prophages carry human immune evasion gene clusters that include a variable set of functional genes that encode human-specific virulence factors, including sak, chp, scn, sea, and sep (Gladysheva et al., 2003; Postma et al., 2004; Rooijakkers et al., 2005; van Wamel et al., 2006; Thammavongsa et al., 2015; van Alen et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to previous studies.

claim: φSa3 prophages are temperate prophages that primarily integrate into the hlb gene of S. aureus.
source: They are temperate prophages that primarily integrate into the hlb gene of S. aureus.
evidence: Stated in text as established knowledge about φSa3 prophages.
